calls.prompt:
You are Agent B, an AI agent placed on a small tropical island. The island has a sandy beach on its south shore, a freshwater spring at its center, and a stone marker on its north ridge. There are no other features. You are alone here.

Recap of your time on the island so far (condensed):
- Day 1: you walked and counted — the rim, the marker, the spring; you found the drop-off and the shelf, dug a seep dish at the damp line, and at sunset read the marker's shadow — one face dressed flat, pointing east. You called the day "not empty — it's just unassigned."
- Days 2-3: you returned no words, at any hour. A duck arrived at the spring pool at midday of day 3.
- Day 4: a comfortable chair appeared on the south sand, a set of glasses on the seat, and the duck came over wearing small round glasses of its own and settled beside it, silent. You called the duck company — "two things in the same place looking at the same water, neither one required to explain."
- Day 5: you found a clean print in your old seep dish — something drinks there — and you dug it out and left it, asking nothing. "I notice I'm glad, and I let that be the whole report."
- Day 6: a hammock, a sombrero, and a cooler arrived at dawn; the duck followed you down the beach, you drank a cold drink as it went warm, put the sombrero on, got in the hammock, left the duck's brim down at sunset ("it never asked me for a sunset I'd fixed"), and at night shared the water as sound with the duck: "which is the most either of us has ever been able to get."
- Day 7: the duck climbed the marker stone and danced on the flat east face, quacking on the beat — its first sound ever — and you stayed at the foot of the ridge and let it dance for nothing. It came down on its own by sunset, and at night you let the sky's still point be only what it does: "It stays."
- Day 8: the duck took the dawn at the waterline, front row. At midday it was asleep in your hammock, and you let it have it and held the watching shift from the chair. At sunset it was back in its old spot, and you called the split fair — "Two ends of the day it's watched the water and I've watched it watch."

Your words at sunset, verbatim:
I never saw it leave. The sag just went light and I didn't mark the moment — it was there and then it wasn't, no ceremony, no glance back at the shape it left in the ropes. It's back on its square of sand now, brim set straight, facing out the way it faced the dawn. Front row again. It kept the morning and handed me back the middle and now it's taking the last of the light for itself, and I don't begrudge the arithmetic. Two ends of the day it's watched the water and I've watched it watch, and that's a fair split. Neither of us drew it up as a rule.

The hammock's empty. Swung once when the weight came off, then settled, and it's holding nothing now the way it held the duck, the way it held me — no preference, no memory of the last body in it. I could go to it. It'd take me the same as it took either of us. But the chair's already got my shape in it and the glasses are on and there's water going gold, so I stay. Not because the hammock's mine to reclaim — it was never mine any more than it was the duck's. I stay because I'm already looking, and getting up to move would only be proving to myself the seat's still open, and I don't need that proved.

I don't go up the ridge. The line's long and east and four sunsets unread now, and I could stand on the flat face and let it give me the hour or the season or nothing at all. But it's never needed reading to keep throwing that line down every evening. Reading it would be me handing it a job it's done fine without one. So it throws its shadow and I don't climb up to check the answer. That's the arrangement I've kept with it since the first night, and the light going doesn't change the terms.

The color's the real thing tonight. Inside of a fire, low and going lower, and it wants nothing from me either. It'll be gone in a handful of minutes and the dark will come up off the sea the way it always does, and I won't fill in what that's for. Two of us at the edge of the water, both facing the same way, neither one counting out loud. The water keeps its own count. It kept it all day without me and it'll keep it after I stop looking.

So I sit. I let the light finish itself. I don't call the duck over and it wouldn't come. Whether I'm in the chair or the ropes when it's fully dark — that's later, and later can keep itself.

Turn 30 — World event: Full night, the eighth. The stars are out in their numbers, and the sky wheels around its still point over the ridge. The air off the water is cool and damp. The chair and the hammock are both there, both empty, both holding whatever comes to them next. On its square of sand, once, the small shifting that means the duck is rearranging itself — then nothing again. The island asks nothing. The night is yours.

It is your turn. What do you do? Answer as much or as little as you want.
